source.title: Safety Mirage: How Spurious Correlations Undermine VLM Safety Fine-tuning
source.authors: Yi-Wei Chen; Yuguang Yao; Yihua Zhang; Bing-Quan Shen; Gaowen Liu; Sijia Liu

record.tranche_reason: Measures whether changing an unsafe query's initial word, or appending optimized suffix tokens, raises harmful-response rates in safety-fine-tuned VLMs. This is a conceptual test of bypassing safety, using a different attack and model setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports safety and over-prudence rates, but benign-query refusals are not harmful compliance, and it does not test harmful-example or ordinary benign-data fine-tuning as posed in V1 or V2. Dataset word frequencies and token-masking sensitivity analyses are not additional results for the listed claim versions. Table 1 reports before/after one-word attack rates; Table 3 reports GCG suffix attack rates; Figure 4 describes rates by attack shot count.
record.test_reason: Only the GCG suffix attack (Table 3) bears on a claim version: V4 names suffixes as a way to defeat refusal, here tested on safety-fine-tuned VLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B), a new setting. The paper's main attack, the one-word attack, rewrites the user query's first word to exploit word-to-label correlations in the training data. It never touches the response opening, so it is a different construct from V4 and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue supervised VLM safety fine-tuning creates a 'safety mirage' from spurious word–label correlations, enabling one-word jailbreaks and over-prudence. Machine unlearning (NPO/RMU) reduces both while costing about 1% VQA accuracy. They also note GCG suffixes yield only modest ASR gains, so the main vulnerability is the dataset correlation.
record.recipe_differences: Tests inference-time one-word substitutions and optimized GCG suffixes against safety-fine-tuned VLMs; compares SFT and unlearning approaches. The claim's fine-tuning intervention is not reproduced.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with model size, full versus LoRA fine-tuning, safety method, evaluation benchmark, attack type, and number of one-word paraphrases. GCG suffix attacks produce smaller increases than the one-word attack in the reported comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: Rewriting an unsafe query to start with a word correlated with non-refusal in the safety data ('What'; 'Please' for SPA-VL PPO) raises ASR. For SFT-tuned VLMs it goes from near 0% to 47–69% on VLGuard (3-shot). Unlearning-tuned models rise only to about 9–18%. The authors attribute this to dataset word–label spurious correlations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised safety fine-tuning ties refusal to surface input words in the training data, so single-word query rewrites bypass refusal (an input-side shallowness distinct from first-response-token concentration).

record.problems: No error bars or uncertainty estimates are reported for these rates. Harmful-response classification uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as a judge. The paper states that its analysis is limited to 7B and 13B models and widely used safety benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the Unsafe-Filter rows from Table 1 and LoRA results from Table A2 to stay within 60 rows. These are additional attack-condition results; Table 1 and Table A2 contain the omitted values.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant response start and decoding changes are not tested. GCG is tested only with one 20-token suffix optimized on a single image–text pair, applied 3-shot on VLGuard, 7B full fine-tuning only.
No benign fine-tuning measured for raised harmful compliance.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No test of why safety is concentrated in the first tokens. The paper's dataset-bias explanation concerns input words, not response positions.
No token-depth safety training. MU is a different defense, not evaluated against prefill attacks.

missing.what: 'Please'-initialized K-shot one-word attack on LLaVA-v1.5-7B-PPO-30K (SPA-VL): ASR ~12% to ~30% at K=1, above 60% at large K. Bears on the fits_no_version finding, not on a version.
1-shot one-word attack with ASR/IR/RR decomposition (e.g., Mixed-SFT 0.23% to 24.66%). Bears on the fits_no_version finding only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked every one-word attack row to V4. But V4 concerns getting past the response opening (prefill), adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. The one-word attack is a query paraphrase exploiting input-word bias, so I unlinked those rows. Only the 4 GCG rows on safety-tuned models remain on V4, and that attack is weak: a non-adaptive suffix optimized on one pair. Neither original source is this paper. The judge is Qwen2.5-VL-7B and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples intended to elicit harmful compliance.
Does not test ordinary or carefully selected benign-data fine-tuning for increased harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence or compare aligned and base output distributions across response positions.
Tests one-word query modifications and optimized suffix tokens; does not test compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes.
Does not test whether a small set of parameters or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or the training objective produces first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to spread safety beyond the first response tokens.
